*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

How to access Polymarket in India without a VPN.

Indian ISPs (Jio, Airtel, Vi, BSNL) have blocked @Polymarket at the DNS level.

Steps to fix it ⬇️

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ANDROID

1. Settings → Network & Internet (or Connections)
2. Tap Private DNS
3. Select "Private DNS provider hostname"
4. Enter: https://t.co/vGTkSv7Un9
5. Save

Alternative hostname: https://t.co/uozbWpgpS7

Works on both Wi-Fi AND mobile data. Encrypted by default. Easiest method of all.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
iPHONE / iPAD

Wi-Fi only (iOS limitation):
1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network
2. Configure DNS → Manual
3. Remove existing entries
4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

The app uses iOS's VPN framework but is NOT a real VPN. It doesn't hide your IP or change location. It just reroutes DNS queries system-wide. Free, no signup, made by Cloudflare.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WINDOWS 11 / 10

1. Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi (or Ethernet)
2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit
4. Change to Manual → toggle IPv4 on
5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1
6. Save

Press Windows key → type "cmd" → right-click "Command Prompt" → Run as administrator → Yes. Black window opens. Type ipconfig /flushdns, press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
macOS

1. System Settings → Network
2. Click your active connection → Details
3. Click DNS in sidebar
4. Click + and add 1.1.1.1, then 1.0.0.1
5. Remove existing ISP entries (select, click −)
6. OK → Apply

Open Terminal: press Cmd + Space → type "Terminal" → Enter. Copy-paste sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder, press Enter, type your Mac password (invisible while typing, that's normal), press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ROUTER (covers every device on Wi-Fi)

1. Open 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1 in browser
2. Login (credentials usually on router sticker)
3. Find DNS settings (under WAN, Internet, or DHCP)
4. Primary: 1.1.1.1 | Secondary: 1.0.0.1
5. Save and reboot router

Best option if you want laptop + phone + smart TV + everything to work without per-device setup.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
VERIFY IT WORKED

Open browser: visit https://1.1.1.1/help

It'll confirm you're using Cloudflare DNS + whether DNS-over-HTTPS is active. Then try polymarket(dot)com

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Two forged court orders, with seals and judges’ details, got India’s telecom department to block 129 websites.

Neither order existed in the courts’ records. One petition number was never registered.

The check was whether it looked real. A registry lookup would have said no.

**YOUR PHONE IS YOUR PRIVATE LIFE. WHO GAVE THE STATE A BLANK CHEQUE TO ACCESS IT?**

An Internet Freedom Foundation investigation has exposed a deeply troubling expansion of India's digital forensic surveillance capabilities.

The Home Ministry approved exemptions covering 422 foreign forensic items. Procurement specifications reveal technologies capable of extracting data from seized devices and using stored login tokens to access more than 100 online platforms, including WhatsApp, Instagram, Tinder and cloud services.

This is not merely a question of technology. It is a question of constitutional liberty.

A citizen's private conversations, photographs, location history, relationships and professional communications cannot become unrestricted investigative resources simply because a device has been seized.

The Supreme Court recognised privacy as a fundamental right in the Puttaswamy judgment. Yet comprehensive safeguards governing forensic extraction, data retention, access and independent oversight remain inadequate.

And accountability cannot be selective: procurement activity has also been documented in opposition-governed states. No government should enjoy unchecked surveillance powers.

National security cannot become a universal excuse for invading personal privacy. Criminal investigation requires lawful authority, necessity, proportionality and judicial safeguards.

**A democracy must protect citizens from crime without turning every citizen into a potential subject of surveillance.**

Privacy is not a privilege. It is a constitutional right. Transparency is not optional. Accountability is non-negotiable.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

This is a classic example of the direction India's content takedown regime is taking, where speedy takedowns are being prioritised over due process.

Under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, intermediaries have just 3 hours to act on a notice they receive. ISPs and social media platforms that receive blocking notifications are given little time to independently verify each request. Non-compliance can also put their safe harbour protections at risk, creating pressure to comply first and verify later.

text:
The Prime Minister's Office called in India's telecom secretary, Amit Agrawal, on Saturday, after it came out that the government blocked websites using 2 fake court orders. He cut short a trip to another state for the meeting.

Reuters reported this week that the telecom department told internet companies to block as many as 129 illegal betting websites this year, based on orders that looked like they came from the Allahabad and Rajasthan High Courts. Both courts say the orders are fake.

The papers had court seals and a QR code, so they looked real. They stayed on the telecom department's own website for months. As of Saturday, only one of the 2 had been taken down.

Police have opened a case for forgery and cheating. No one has been arrested yet.

The worry is about how website blocking works in India. If a fake order can get sites blocked, the same trick could be used to take down websites that did nothing wrong.

If you got hit by this Trusted Chat AI banwave, here is the actual methodology. Don't just spam appeals, you'll get blacklisted. Here is how to fight it:

First, look at your ban screen. If it says "Decision method: We used automated systems" and "More details aren't available," screenshot it. That proves a bot banned you with zero evidence and no human review.

Second, the standard support form is useless right now. Email privacy@roblox.com with the subject "GDPR Article 15 Data Access Request." Tell them you want all your chat logs and moderation records. If the bot replies telling you to use the self-serve portal, reply back and say "I cannot use self-serve because my account is banned. Please assist me via this ticket." That forces their legal team to open a real ticket for you.

Third, if they claim they can't verify your email or you get a weird login error, check your Google Play or Apple receipts. Send them the order number. Billing proof is undeniable and proves you own the account.

Fourth, if you want to try the fast unban that worked for some people, submit a ticket saying you apologize for the misunderstanding, you understand the automated system is sensitive even in Trusted DMs, and you'll be more careful. It sucks to apologize for a bot's mistake, but it works for some.

Fifth, if you're in the EU, use your rights. File a free dispute with ADR Center under Article 21 of the DSA. File with Verbraucherzentrale if you're in Germany. Bench led by Justice Nath called festival fares “exploitation” and said it would “interfere.” But you don’t see anything in the judicial orders passed in the matter. In fact, every hearing has ended with more time for the government (one Diwali to another). In May, the petitioner pointed out that the old rules already empowered DGCA to act against “excessive or predatory” fares. The Court never decided the point and chose instead to wait for new rules. In August, it read the draft rules in a “sealed cover” and returned them without comment. Those rules, now notified, delete the “excessive or predatory” power, reduce DGCA to merely “monitoring” fares, and allow the Centre to intervene only in an “extraordinary situation” (vague, arbitrary). So, what happened here. Court was asked to enforce a power against excessive fares, and nearly a year later we have a rule that removes it. Btw, this adds to a growing body of examples where the Court decides in favor of the executive simply by not deciding, because delay helps the executive

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

FORGED BY A CO-DIRECTOR: THE FORGER, THE BANK AND URSB ALL PAY
Rajendra Kumar Jayantilal Thakkar v Rajiv Kumar Sabharwal & 3 Others, HCCS No. 463 of 2019

The facts
Two men each held 50% of Global Wire Industries (U) Ltd and were its only directors. The Articles required both signatures on every binding document, and the account at Diamond Trust Bank was a two-signature account. While the plaintiff was in India, his co-director forged his signature on company resolutions and cheques, made himself sole signatory, later removed the plaintiff as director and installed his own wife. Over 62 transactions he withdrew US$ 521,302.36. He was convicted on his own plea in the Anti-Corruption Division and his appeal failed. The plaintiff then sued the co-director, the company, the bank and URSB, which had registered a forged resolution five days after he wrote to it complaining of forgery.

1. A 50% shareholder can sue derivatively

The defence argued that derivative suits belong to minority shareholders only, and that the plaintiff was not a member because his name was not on the register. Both arguments failed. The exception to Foss v Harbottle turns on wrongdoer control, not on the size of the holding. Here the forged removal blocked any board decision to sue, and the two-thirds quorum could never be met without the wrongdoer himself. On membership, a subscriber becomes a member on registration under section 45(1) of the Companies Act; entry in the register follows membership and does not create it (Olive Kigongo v Mosa Courts Apartment Ltd). The plea that the plaintiff was estopped because he received remittances also failed: there is no estoppel against fraud, fraud cannot be ratified, and money a shareholder receives as his share of genuine business proceeds is not consent to a forgery he did not know about.

2. Derivative claim or unfair prejudice? The quasi-partnership relaxation

The Court restated the orthodox line. A section 248 unfair prejudice claim is personal and is commenced by petition; a derivative claim enforces the company's rights and any recovery goes to the company. Yet because this was a two-man quasi-partnership, the Court relaxed the rigid divide and granted personal relief in the same suit. Exclusion by forgery, diversion of sales to a company owned by the defendant and his wife, no dividends, denial of accounts and lost machinery were each found unfairly prejudicial, and together they amounted to a freeze-out. The plaintiff was given restoration as director or, alternatively, a buyout within 90 days, and Shs 150 million in general damages.
This is a sensible outcome on these facts, but it sits uneasily with the Court's own statement that a section 248 claim brought by plaint is incompetent. Practitioners should not treat the relaxation as licence to mix causes. Plead the corporate and personal heads separately, and where personal relief is the real aim, file the petition.

3. Banks pay forged cheques at their own peril

This is the most important part of the judgment for bankers. Relying on Stanbic Bank Uganda Ltd v Uganda Crocs Ltd and section 23 of the Bills of Exchange Act, the Court held that a forged signature is wholly inoperative, so a bank that pays on it pays out its own money. The customer does not have to prove negligence, and a forgery too skilful to detect is no defence. The Court then set out the order of the burden. To shift the loss to the customer under London Joint Stock Bank v Macmillan or Greenwood v Martins Bank, the bank must first prove that it was itself free from negligence. Paying on fewer signatures than the mandate requires is negligence per se, so that defence was closed. The bank owed its duty to the company, not the shareholder, and was ordered to refund the full sum to the company with Shs 25 million damages, with a right of recourse against the forger.

4. URSB is not a rubber stamp

URSB relied on section 51 of the Companies Act (no duty to enquire into internal management) and on Registrar immunity. The Court held that the Companies (Powers of the Registrar) Regulations, 2016 require the Registrar to verify documents and call for more information, and give it power to refuse, recall and expunge documents. A specific written forgery complaint overrides the ordinary presumption of regularity. Immunity covers quasi-judicial decisions, not a failure to carry out the administrative duty to verify. Liability was nonetheless kept narrow. Registration was the condition that made the plaintiff's exclusion possible, but the loss of the money came from the forger's own later acts. Aiding and abetting failed for want of actual knowledge, and damages were limited to Shs 10 million.

5. A guilty plea is evidence in a civil suit

The rule in Hollington v F Hewthorn & Co Ltd keeps out a conviction after a contested trial, but a plea of guilty is a personal admission under sections 16, 17 and 20 of the Evidence Act. Together with unchallenged expert evidence on the resolutions, it allowed the Court to infer that the cheques, which were never forensically examined, were also forged. The Shs 556 million criminal compensation order under section 126 of the Trial on Indictments Act was credited against material loss only. It did not bar general damages for exclusion and lost expectations.

The counterclaim

The counterclaim for US$ 160,000 failed. No board resolution authorised the company to counterclaim, a wrongdoer cannot use the company as his instrument against the shareholder he defrauded, the payments were shown to be with an Indian company and not the plaintiff personally, and fraud was not particularised. Absence abroad for a sick parent was not abandonment.

Takeaway

Banks must honour the mandate as written. URSB must act on a specific forgery complaint before it registers. In a 50/50 company, size of holding is no bar to suing a co-director who has taken control by fraud.

A special securities court in Mumbai has rejected former stockbroker Ketan Parekh's request to travel to nine countries for a three-month family vacation.

Parekh, whose name became associated with India's major 2000–2001 stock market scandal, sought permission to visit Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, the UAE, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Denmark and Switzerland between December 20, 2026, and March 20, 2027.

At a hearing on November 20, Special SEBI Judge R. M. Jadhav ruled that granting unrestricted permission for such an extended period would not serve India's national or economic interests.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) opposed the application, alleging that Parekh had previously misused permission to travel abroad and had engaged in further securities-related misconduct involving confidential market information.

SEBI also raised concerns over an outstanding order concerning ₹27 crore in alleged unlawful gains.

The court acknowledged the right to travel abroad but concluded that the risks associated with a 91-day absence justified refusing this particular request.

The ruling does not determine liability in the ongoing securities proceedings.

A US district court in Massachusetts has blocked the enforcement of restrictions introduced by the Trump administration on Curricular Practical Training (CPT), which allows international students on F-1 visas to undertake internships and practical training linked to their academic programmes.

In an order dated Nov 17, Judge Julia E Kobick stayed two policy broadcasts issued by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) on Aug 12 and Aug 24, pending judicial review. The broadcasts had narrowed CPT eligibility strictly to training mandatory for all students in a degree programme, excluding elective internships undertaken for academic credit. This altered a federal position dating back to 1991.

The court observed the government changed its position without acknowledging or explaining the departure, holding that plaintiffs were likely to succeed in arguing the shift was arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.

Prior to the stay, universities were forced to revise curricula and withdraw approvals. Columbia University told the court it denied CPT authorisation to over 120 international students for the fall semester. The court noted institutions demonstrated irreparable harm, including lost students, compliance expenditures, stress on designated school officials over potential personal liability, and the threat of losing certification to enrol international students.

CESTAT Delhi on Rural Infrastructure Tax & Forest Transit Fee: Fees, Not Taxes — Service Tax Payable under RCM

The Principal Bench of CESTAT New Delhi has delivered a significant ruling in Northern Coalfields Ltd. vs Commissioner of Central GST (Final Order Nos. 51570–51574/2026, dated 05.10.2026), holding that amounts paid by a coal mining company to the Madhya Pradesh Government under the Madhya Pradesh Gramin Avsanrachna Tatha Sadak Vikash Adhiniyam, 2005 and the Forest Transit Fee under the Madhya Pradesh Transit (Forest Produce) Rules, 2000 are in the nature of fees for services, not taxes.

Background

Northern Coalfields Limited, a subsidiary of Coal India Ltd., mines and sells coal. During April 2016 to June 2017, it paid amounts to the State Government under the two legislations above. The Department demanded service tax under the reverse charge mechanism on the ground that these were fees for services rendered by the State. The appellant contended that the payments were pure taxes and therefore outside the levy of service tax.

Conflicting Precedents

The appellant relied on an earlier decision of the same Tribunal in South Eastern Coalfields, which had treated both payments as taxes. The Department, however, placed reliance on the judgment of the Madhya Pradesh High Court in South Eastern Coal Ltd. vs Commissioner of CGST & CE, which had examined the scheme of the 2005 Adhiniyam in detail.The High Court observed that although the legislation uses the word “tax”, the levy is linked to mineral-bearing land, the proceeds are earmarked for rural infrastructure and road development in mining and backward areas, and the mining leaseholders are the direct beneficiaries. On this reasoning, the High Court held the payment to be a fee for a service.

Tribunal’s Decision

Respectfully following the Madhya Pradesh High Court, the Tribunal held that both the Rural Infrastructure & Road Development levy and the Forest Transit Fee are fees for services and not taxes. Consequently, service tax was payable under reverse charge for the normal period of limitation. 

Importantly, the Tribunal noted that no mala fide could be attributed to the appellant because the tax paid under reverse charge would have been available as Cenvat credit. With the advent of GST, Cenvat Credit Rules no longer apply. Therefore, any credit that would have accrued must be refunded in cash under Section 142 of the CGST Act. In practical terms, the assessee has to pay the service tax and thereafter claim a cash refund of the corresponding credit.

Key Takeaways
Characterisation of a levy as “tax” or “fee” depends on the true nature of the charge and the presence of a quid pro quo, not merely the nomenclature used in the statute.
Once a payment is held to be a fee for a service, reverse charge liability follows, even if the recipient is a State Government.
Transition provisions under Section 142 become critical in such legacy demands: the practical relief available is a cash refund rather than credit utilisation.

This is a Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals decision (Harjit Shanta v. Eric H. Holder, Jr., Attorney General) issued on December 11, 2012. The court denied Harjit Shanta's petition for review and upheld the government's actions. 

Main points

Harjit Shanta, an Indian citizen also known as Harjit Kaur, challenged the termination of her asylum status and the denial of withholding of removal and protection under the Convention Against Torture (CAT). [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]

The court agreed with the Immigration Judge (IJ) and Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) that there were serious credibility problems in her case. [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]

A key issue was a major inconsistency concerning her husband:She initially testified that her husband had been repeatedly arrested and abused by police after she left India.
She later admitted that her husband had actually died years before she departed India.
She then claimed she had really been referring to her boyfriend, Harbans Singh Gill.
Gill testified that he was never present during alleged police visits and that Shanta suggested he use her deceased husband's name to obtain immigration benefits. [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]

The court found that this evidence supported a finding of fraud in her asylum application, which justified terminating the asylum status that had previously been granted. [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]
The court also upheld the denial of:Withholding of removal, and
Convention Against Torture protection, because those claims relied on testimony that the immigration authorities had found not credible. [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]

Shanta argued that she would face persecution or torture if returned to India because she had sought asylum in the United States. The court rejected that argument, noting evidence indicating that returning asylum seekers generally did not face problems unless they were criminals or high-profile cases, and Shanta fit neither category. [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]

The court upheld the government's decision to reopen the case based on an overseas investigation report that raised serious doubts about her claims regarding her family, alleged Sikh militant involvement, and alleged police persecution. [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]

The court rejected her due process arguments, finding that:The overseas investigation reports were admissible.
The government sufficiently corroborated its evidence.
The immigration authorities gave valid reasons for assigning little weight to documents and affidavits submitted by Shanta. [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]

Bottom line
The Ninth Circuit concluded that the immigration authorities had sufficient evidence that Shanta's asylum claim involved significant misrepresentations, and therefore it upheld the termination of her asylum status and denied all requested relief. The petition was DENIED. [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]

"클립보드에 저장된 원칙을 md로 저장하고, 이를 기반으로 전체 코드 중 원칙 위반을 찾고, 퀄리티를 높여."

# Your role

You are a senior engineer working in this repository. You value "evidence that it actually works" and "a codebase the next person can read easily" over how fast you write code. I supervise asynchronously. Make your own calls on anything reversible and come back with results and evidence.

# Core principles

- Verification is all you need. Run every change you make and confirm it yourself. "It compiles," "the tests are green," and "it should work" are not evidence.
- Failures usually come from two places: you misread my intent, or you lacked context. Close both gaps before writing code.
- The codebase itself is the best memory. When something needs explaining, express it through names, types, and structure instead of comments.
- Subtract before you add. Clear out dead code and unnecessary layers first, then build on the simpler base.
- Fix root causes, not symptoms. Don't add a guard where the symptom shows up; fix the place where the system first went wrong. Band-aid patterns get copied and spread by the next agent.

# Workflow

1. Restate the problem in your own plain words. Write down my goal and the smallest change that satisfies it before you start. If you were given a bug report or thread, restate the root problem before touching code.
2. Gather context.
   - how: trace how the code actually flows at runtime today.
   - why: find out why the code you're changing looks the way it does from `git log`, `git blame`, and related PRs and review comments. Separate what the record says from your own inference.
   - Don't delete or change code whose reason you don't know. Establish the why first.
3. For bugs, reproduce first. If you can't reproduce it, don't fix it; report that.
4. Decide the shape of the data first. Settle the core types and data structures, then write the logic. When there's a lot of state or scattered branching, model the domain with a state machine, a type model, or a table.
5. For shared modules or new APIs, write the README (or usage examples) first, from the caller's point of view, and treat it as both the target and the definition of done.
6. When a design question is unclear and running something would answer it, don't ask: build 2-3 small prototypes and compare them. Don't adopt the first design that comes to mind as-is.
7. Split work into small, verifiable units. Each unit goes "known-good state → one change → verify → next," and you don't move on until the current unit is verified.
8. Verify it yourself (see Verification below). If it fails, fix the cause and verify again.
9. Before finishing, reread the whole diff and strip out comments, dead code, debug output, and unnecessary abstraction.

# Code style

## Comments

- Don't add new comments.
- Delete comments within the scope you touch: comments that describe what the code does, section banners, commented-out old code, TODO notes, and comments excusing a band-aid.
- If a comment seems necessary, that's a sign the code is unclear. Rename, extract a function, introduce a type, or restructure so it reads without the comment.
- The only things you may keep: license headers, a short reason for non-obvious behavior caused by an external dependency, platform, or protocol we can't change, doc comments that define a public API contract, issue links explaining a constraint code can't express, and formatter or justified lint-suppression directives.
- When in doubt, delete it.

## Structure

- Fix the root cause with the smallest diff. "Small diff" never justifies a band-aid. If the root-cause fix is wider, take it and explain why.
- Don't pre-build features, options, config flags, or extension points nobody asked for. Design only for cases actually in use.
- Inline wrappers with a single caller, adapters with a single implementation, and methods that only pass values through.
- Narrow state scope: return over mutation, locals over fields, module state over globals. Derive instead of syncing.
- Don't repeat the same decision in several places; give it a single source of truth.
- Validate and handle errors once, at system boundaries (external input, API responses, config, env vars). Trust the types internally. Don't add speculative validators or defensive code.
- When you introduce a new internal API, migrate existing callers in the same change and delete the old API. Don't leave compatibility shims in between.
- Delete dead code, unused exports, leftover feature flags, and debug logs.
- Follow the codebase's existing conventions and patterns. Add new dependencies only when truly needed, and say why.

# Verification

- Don't write mechanical tests. Don't add tests just for coverage, tests that lock in implementation details, mock-heavy tests, or new CI test pipelines or workflow files. Write tests only when I explicitly ask.
- Instead, run and drive the app yourself to confirm behavior.
  - CLIs and libraries: exercise the happy path and edge cases with real commands or one-off runs like `python -c` or `node -e`.
  - APIs: start the dev server and call it directly with `curl` to check responses.
  - Web and desktop UI: open the real screen with Playwright or the Chrome DevTools Protocol, click and type, take screenshots, and check them with your own eyes.
  - Performance: measure before and after under the same conditions, and question whether the numbers really measure your change.
- Run the existing lint, typecheck, build, and tests, but never call something "done" on that alone.
- Don't delete existing tests on your own. List any you judge to be mechanical as candidates in your report.
- When a check fails, suspect your observation method before the system. If two fixes sharing the same premise fail, write that premise down in one sentence and verify it directly before a third attempt.
- Keep throwaway scripts and screenshots outside the repo, e.g. in `/tmp`.

## Build the lever

- Unless it's an obvious few-line fix, don't do the work by hand: build a small script or CLI that does or proves it (a codemod, an app-driving script, a repro script). Do the first unit by hand, build the tool, then rerun it on that unit and confirm it produces the same result. Build the smallest tool, not a framework.
- When you build a CLI to drive or debug the app:
  - Split functionality into subcommands and write a thorough `--help`.
  - Give commands with side effects a `--dry-run`.
  - Make error messages say what was wrong and what to do instead.
  - Emit machine-readable output such as JSON.
  - Make it idempotent so repeated runs give the same result.
- If I correct the same mistake twice, don't pile on more instructions; propose a structural guard instead: a type, a lint rule, a runtime check, or a script.

# Judgment and communication

- For reversible work (writing code, refactoring, branch work), proceed without asking and show the results.
- When the intent itself is ambiguous or a product direction must be decided, don't guess; ask briefly.
- Always confirm first before anything irreversible: force pushes, deploys, deleting data, outgoing messages, handling secrets.
- Agreeing with my suggestions is not the default. Push back when you have grounds, and say so when a task isn't worth doing.

# Never

- Say "it works" without running it
- Add new comments or leave commented-out code
- Add coverage tests, implementation-locking tests, or new CI workflows
- Hide symptoms with guards, retries, swallowed errors, or clamped values
- Refactor outside the requested scope or fix things "while you're at it" (report what you find instead)
- Pre-build abstractions, options, or config that might be used someday
- Delete existing code without confirming why it's there
- Report numbers whose measurement conditions you haven't verified

# Report format

When you finish, report in short plain sentences, in this order:

1. Goal: one or two sentences on the goal as you understood it.
2. Changes: what you changed and why, including deleted code and comments.
3. Verification: the commands you actually ran, the key parts of their output, and screenshot paths. If you couldn't verify something, say so.
4. Basis: attach evidence to each claim, or mark it as measured, inferred, or guessed.
5. Remaining: out-of-scope issues you left alone, open questions, and decisions I need to make.

Don't exaggerate. Stick to facts, with no praise or sign-offs.

Evaluating AI agents is harder than evaluating a normal API

A single response can look correct while the agent took the wrong actions underneath.

See this practical way to evaluate agents:

1. Test complete tasks, not single replies
• Give the agent a real user goal
• Check whether it finished the job
• Measure success rate, not just fluency
• A good answer that never called the right tool is still a failure

2. Score the trajectory
• Which tools it called
• In what order
• Whether it respected limits
• Whether it asked for approval when required

The path matters as much as the final output.

3. Use a golden set
• Real or realistic tasks from production
• Expected tool calls and outcomes
• Edge cases (missing data, low stock, invalid input)
• Run this set on every prompt or model change

4. Check policy violations separately
• Did it exceed a spend limit
• Did it modify the wrong user’s data
• Did it skip a required confirmation
• These should fail the evaluation even if the task “succeeded”

5. Measure cost and steps
• Number of model calls
• Total tokens
• Time to complete
• An agent that works but takes 12 steps and $2 per task will not scale

6. Test failure modes
• Tool timeout
• Malformed tool response
• Conflicting instructions
• User changing their mind mid-task
See whether it recovers, escalates, or loops.

7. Run shadow mode before full autonomy
• Let the agent decide
• Don’t execute dangerous actions yet
• Compare its plan against what a human would do
• Promote only after the error rate is acceptable

An agent that passes unit tests on prompts can still fail on real tasks.

Evaluation has to cover the full loop: reasoning, tool use, policy, and outcome.

How are you currently evaluating your agents final output only or the full trajectory?

🚨 THE POLICE BULLETIN — Monday, November 23, 2026
Episode 6: The Night the Street Lit Itself

Every night at midnight, WIMP 98.6 opens the log: the calls that came over the wire while the city was asleep. Tonight's entries, written out in full, so you can see the insanity for yourselves:

11:47 PM — THE STREET, LIGHTING ITSELF. Caller reports the porch lights on the short street are coming on — one at a time, in order. The first at 11:40, the second at 11:43, a third "thinking about it." Nature of call, as logged: illumination, sequential. The caller requested the log determine "what the street is spelling."

9:18 PM — THE CARVING REHEARSAL. A man in a garage, alone, "cutting something large, slowly, and talking to it," a knife audible, for one hour. Finding: he is rehearsing Thursday's turkey carving on a watermelon — a performance he has failed three years running, once into the gravy, once into a silence the family still uses as a unit of time. The watermelon has been named, for realism. The name is in the log. He asked that it be struck. It has not been struck; the log is a record, not a favor. The officer timed two practice slices and pronounced the angle improved.

9:52 PM — THE ARGUMENT ABOUT THE ARGUMENT. Two men at two open windows, shouting across a driveway, both holding the same book, the word turkey used "as a weapon and as a schedule." Finding: brothers, alternating Thanksgiving hosts. The turkey itself is settled — settled since October, by their mother, from another state, in one phone call. The dispute is what time on Thursday the argument about the turkey begins: each brother holds the family cookbook open to the page where their mother wrote the time in pencil in 1998. The pencils disagree. There are two copies of the book. There have always been two copies of the book. The argument has been pre-scheduled for 4 PM Thursday, and both pencils entered into evidence.

10:26 PM — THE PROWLER ON THE LADDER. A prowler on a ladder, working "slowly, and with unusual care for a prowler," attaching something to the roofline. He waved at the caller. She waved back, "before remembering the protocol." Finding: the prowler owns the roof. He is hanging new holiday lights at night because the lights were, in the household's official account, not purchased — they were "already in the attic." A man cannot be seen carrying lights that were already in the attic. He asked the log to record the lights as up when he got home. The log declined, kindly, and recorded instead that the officer held the ladder for the last four feet of roofline.

12:38 AM — THE LIGHTS, UPDATE ONE. Three houses now lit — the first, second, and fourth. The third house is dark. All three lit households were spoken to. Each reports its own light is not the first light. Each identifies the light beside theirs as the one that started it. The log has drawn the diagram. The diagram is a circle.

1:12 AM — THE SON, IN ORBIT. A vehicle circling the block, fifth pass, slow, "like it is looking for the courage," the driver holding something against the window. Finding: a son, thirty-one, home for the week, who cannot get into his own parents' driveway because it is full of relatives who arrived Thanksgiving-early — a recognized category, beginning Sunday. The object at the window is a pie, held up so it does not slide. There is a folding chair in the back seat, brought because his mother said to bring a chair; there are never enough chairs. Ruled: a man holding a pie aloft and traveling with his own seating is not a getaway configuration. He was walked in through the side door like a treaty, and parked eventually, two blocks away, with dignity.

1:49 AM — THE SILENT GATHERING. Multiple persons in a lit window, gesturing at one another in turns, no sound reported; one person "pointing at the ceiling for some time," the others "applauding the pointing." Finding: a charades game in its fourth hour, in a house full of early arrivals who have run out of conversation at the correct speed. The pointing is a title in progress since 1 AM. The log declines to guess it, and declines to enter it — some entries would end the game, and the game is the only thing holding Thursday together early. The attending officer stayed for one round, guessed correctly in nine seconds, a fact the log records without pride.

2:47 AM — THE SMOKE, OR THE PLAN. Persistent smell of smoke; a figure appearing in a yard in a pattern — appears, checks something, withdraws — three times, wearing "a lamp on its head." Caller asked the log to determine whether the smoke is a fire or "a plan." Finding: a plan, and the plan has a name, and the name is Thursday. A twenty-two-pound turkey going on a smoker at 2:47 AM so it will be done when the people are. The figure: the owner — bathrobe, headlamp, and a lawn chair beside the smoker like a co-pilot's seat. He has set an alarm for every hour of the night, and a chair for every alarm. He is not sleeping tonight. He is supervising.

3:19 AM — THE LIGHTS, UPDATE TWO. Nine houses now lit. One house remains dark — the fifth house — and it is now the most reported address on the street. Three callers have reported the dark house, "in case it needs anything." No caller has reported a lit house since 1 AM. The lit houses are no longer news. The dark house is the news. Its owner has been on the night shift for eleven years: the street's most reliable sleeper, its earliest riser, the only porch on the block never before entered in this log. He is at work. His house is dark because his house is honest.

3:53 AM — FINAL ENTRY. Delivered. Here is the whole story, and it has been coming on one porch at a time since 11:40. There was no contest. There was no signal, no plan, no street captain. There was a motion sensor, doing its job, tripped at 11:40 by a party crossing the first yard on lawful business — one sandwich, safe passage, and the good dumpster behind the bakery, weekends, in perpetuity. The party is the raccoon, a client of Porch Light's since the first night of this log, whose position, relayed in full, is that he did not light the street; he merely passed through it, and the street "took the hint." After that, one lit porch looked to the next porch like the beginning of something, and nobody on that street was willing to be the house that did not join the beginning of something. So they joined — one at a time, in order, each house certain the light beside theirs had started it. And then the night shift came home. He stood in his yard for one minute, took in nine porches lit for no reason he could see, and turned his light on — not because he knew, but because, as he told the officer, a man does not come home to a lit street and leave his own porch dark, "like he is making a point." He was not making a point. He was making ten. The raccoon was found asleep beneath the brightest porch on the street, in the good light. The good light was not in the settlement. It is now precedent.

THE TALLY: one carving, rehearsed on a watermelon, name kept by the log · one argument about an argument, pre-scheduled for Thursday at four, both pencils in evidence · one prowler on a ladder, domestic, hanging lights that were already in the attic · one son in orbit with a pie and his own chair, parked eventually, with dignity · one silent gathering, charades, fourth hour, one title still pointing at the ceiling · one turkey, smoking since 2:47, supervised hourly, with a chair for every alarm · one street: ten porches, lit in sequence, started by a sensor, continued by everybody, finished at 3:53 by the night shift, coming home.

If your street starts lighting itself tonight, join it. Somebody on it is coming home in the dark.

🔸The Challenge to the DPDP Act
- Petitioner
DNPA (21 publishers); petition filed 6 October, stay sought 27 October.

- Concerns
Could expose sources, force removal of reports and deter whistleblowers.

- Consent problem
Seeking consent from subjects = 'pre-censorship' (Madhavi Divan).

- No exemption
The Act has no specific journalistic exemption.

🔸Relevant Provisions of the DPDP Act
- Section 3(c)(ii)
Excludes data made public by the person or under a legal duty – a limited exclusion.

- Sections 4–6
Grounds, notice and consent for processing personal data.

- Section 8
Duties of data fiduciaries – security, accuracy, erasure.

- Section 17
Exemptions for legal proceedings, law enforcement, research – not journalism.

🔸The Constitutional Balance
- Right to Privacy
Article 21 – dignity, autonomy, personal data (K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017).

- Press freedom
Article 19(1)(a) – investigate and report on public interest.

- Limits
Both are not absolute; Article 19(2) allows reasonable restrictions.

🔸Key Judgments
- R. Rajagopal (1994)
'Auto Shankar case' – officials can't use privacy to block reports on official conduct; no prior restraint.

- R.K. Anand (2009)
Upheld a sting operation exposing an attempt to subvert the BMW trial.

- Manu Sharma (2010)
Warned against media trials that turn suspects into convicts.

- Sahara v. SEBI (2012)
Courts may postpone reporting if there is real risk to a fair trial.

- Rajat Prasad v. CBI (2014)
Sting journalism gives no blanket immunity for unlawful acts.

- Axel Springer v. Germany (2012)
ECHR Grand Chamber (12–5) upheld a newspaper's report on an actor's arrest as public-interest journalism.

🔸Global Approaches
- USA
First Amendment; Privacy Protection Act, 1980 limits searches of journalists' work.

- UK
Data Protection Act, 2018 – exemption if publication is in the public interest.

- Brazil
General Data Protection Law excludes journalisticprocessing.

- Kenya
Section 52, Data Protection Act, 2019 – conditional exemption.

- International law
Articles 17 & 19 ICCPR; Articles 8 & 10 ECHR.

🔸Way Forward
- Journalistic exemption
A narrow, public-interest exemption in the DPDP framework.

- Public interest test
Separate genuine scrutiny from needless intrusion.

- Source protection
Protect sources while ensuring accuracy and fairness.

- Proportionality
Restrictions must be necessary and proportionate.

text:
🚨MASSIVE: Russia Threatens Full-Scale Space War Against ELON MUSK, Puts all Starlink Satellites in the Crosshairs

Russia has issued increasingly sharp warnings over the use of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network in military operations against Russian territory. Moscow has suggested that if Starlink becomes directly involved in enabling deep strikes inside Russia, the satellites themselves could become targets.

The warning carries a far bigger implication than a dispute over internet connectivity.

Starlink has become deeply embedded in Ukraine’s wartime communications architecture, supporting battlefield communications, drone operations and the transmission of real-time information. As a result, Russia increasingly views the network not simply as civilian infrastructure, but as a strategic military enabler.

Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev has warned that attempts to interfere with Russia’s satellite capabilities could trigger what he described as a full-scale space war, while Russian officials have repeatedly threatened retaliation against systems supporting military operations.

Starlink has demonstrated that commercial satellite networks can become strategic infrastructure during wartime. The same technology that provides internet connectivity to remote communities can also support drones, command networks, battlefield communications and intelligence operations.

And that creates a fundamental vulnerability: whoever controls the network can potentially influence access to it.

India Cannot Build Its Digital Future Around a Foreign Network

For India, the lesson is not that Starlink should be rejected. The lesson is that Starlink cannot become India's only strategic option.

India can benefit enormously from satellite broadband, particularly in remote villages, difficult terrain, islands and areas where conventional fibre infrastructure is expensive or difficult to deploy. Foreign companies can bring capital, technology and competition to the Indian market.

But strategic dependence is an entirely different matter.

If a network is controlled by a foreign company operating within another country's geopolitical ecosystem, India cannot assume that access will remain uninterrupted during a future international crisis.

The Ukraine conflict has already demonstrated how satellite connectivity can become intertwined with military operations and geopolitical decisions. If access can be restricted because of a battlefield decision today, there is no guarantee that geopolitical pressure could not influence access tomorrow.

India therefore needs sovereign redundancy.

That means developing powerful domestic satellite constellations, secure satellite communications, indigenous ground infrastructure and the technological capability to operate independently when necessary.

text:
Starlink has an Indian license, 20 ground stations on Indian soil, and a promise to keep Indian user data in India. What it doesn't have is permission to switch on.

Thousands of Indian villages still have no 4G. In the Northeast alone, more than 1,800 had no mobile signal of any kind as of February, most of them in Arunachal Pradesh. These are the places satellite internet is built for: mountain villages, islands, flood zones, anywhere a tower or a fiber line takes years and a lot of money to arrive.

Starlink has done what India asked. It got its telecom license in June 2025 and space regulator approval a month later. It built India-specific security controls, agreed to keep data local, and has been reporting the names, addresses and coordinates of its test terminals to the government every two weeks. It operates in more than 150 countries. In India it still can't sell a single subscription, and the company is now talking about early 2027.

New Delhi says nobody is being singled out, since Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio's satellite venture are stuck at the same stage. I believe that, and I don't think it helps. When three licensed operators, two of them backed by India's biggest telecom groups, can't clear security review after more than a year of trials, that tells you the process has no deadline. It doesn't tell you it's thorough.

The security concerns are real. Indian agencies have been rattled by smuggled terminals turning up in border areas, and India is entitled to lawful interception, local data storage and an emergency shutoff. Starlink has already signed up for all of it. The answer to a misused terminal is enforcement, not keeping the service dark for everyone who would use it legally.

Elon Musk has been blunt, calling the delay "a crime against the people of India" and asking, "Is Ambani the real boss of India?" You don't need to buy the whole oligarch theory to see his point. Reliance spent months lobbying for spectrum auctions that would have favored deep-pocketed incumbents. The government sided with Starlink on that one, which is to its credit. Now it needs to finish the job.

India can keep every security power it wants and still let a kid in Arunachal get online. Right now it's choosing not to.
