Text of My Keynote Address
Delivered at the National Press Day, 2026 celebrations organised by the National Union of Journalists (India), Hyderabad, on 16 November 2026.

*****

Distinguished office-bearers of the National Union of Journalists (India), members of the journalist fraternity, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen.

My greetings to all of you on #NationalPressDay2026.

I am delighted to address an issue that goes beyond the interests of journalists and media organisations. It concerns the survival of truth, the accountability of power and the foundations of democracy.

Artificial Intelligence is transforming how information is created and disseminated—and how people perceive reality. It offers extraordinary possibilities but also unprecedented dangers. In an age when reality itself can be manufactured, who will defend the truth?

For journalism, this is not merely a technological challenge. It is a test of credibility, independence and courage.

I would like to examine this challenge from a democratic and constitutional perspective.

1. AI AND THE MANUFACTURE OF REALITY

Every major technological revolution has transformed communication. The printing press expanded the dissemination of knowledge; radio and television transformed mass communication; the internet removed geographical barriers. Artificial Intelligence takes this transformation to an entirely different level.

Today, videos, voices, photographs, documents and entire narratives can be fabricated and presented as authentic. The consequences can be devastating: elections manipulated, reputations destroyed, social unrest provoked, national security threatened and the administration of justice compromised.

Yet AI can also assist journalism by analysing vast volumes of information, identifying patterns, translating Indian languages and helping uncover facts.
But one distinction is fundamental: the ability to manufacture information is not the ability to establish truth.

A convincing video is not necessarily genuine evidence. An algorithmically identified pattern is not proof of wrongdoing. A machine can generate a narrative, but it cannot assume responsibility for its veracity.

Verification, corroboration and independent human judgment remain indispensable.

AI may transform the tools of journalism. It must never be allowed to manufacture the truth that journalism is duty-bound to discover.

2. THE PRESS AND DEMOCRACY

A functioning democracy rests on four great institutions: the Legislature, the Executive, the Judiciary and the Free Press. The first three are constitutional organs of the State. The Press has evolved as the Fourth Estate, performing an equally indispensable democratic function.

Our National Emblem offers an interesting metaphor. The Lion Capital of Ashoka depicts four lions standing back to back. Three are visible; the fourth remains invisible. One could metaphorically associate that invisible fourth lion with the Press—not as a constitutional interpretation, but as a reminder of its indispensable democratic role.

The Legislature makes laws, the Executive implements them and the Judiciary interprets them and safeguards the rule of law. The Press informs citizens, scrutinises power, exposes wrongdoing and gives voice to public concerns.

It is the bridge between governance and the people, telling citizens what is done in their name, with their mandate and, most importantly, with their money.

Article 19(1)(a) of our Constitution guarantees freedom of speech and expression. The Supreme Court has recognised freedom of the Press as integral to this right, subject to the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).

Press freedom is not merely a professional privilege. It is also the citizen's right to receive information and form independent opinions.

The Press is not merely an observer of democracy. It enables citizens to question power and hold those who govern them accountable.

3. MEDIA INDEPENDENCE: FROM WHOM AND WHAT?

We frequently discuss press freedom in terms of censorship, governmental interference and intimidation. But the question of independence goes much deeper.

Independence from whom? Independence from what?

Is the Press independent of governments, political parties, corporate owners, commercial interests, ideological and religious influences? Is it independent of its own prejudices?

A Press free from governmental censorship but controlled by political patrons, corporate owners or ideological loyalties is not truly independent.

First: Independence from political ownership and control.

Political parties, politicians and their associates own, control or influence media organisations. At the same time, business interests increasingly enter politics, while politicians acquire commercial interests.
When business becomes politics and politics becomes business, the media becomes an instrument through which both protect their power and interests.

The expression Godi Media has become a widely used pejorative description of sections of the Indian mainstream media since 2014. It reflects the criticism that sections of the media have been manipulated, subdued or co-opted into functioning as publicity and propaganda instruments for the RSS-BJP political establishment and Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The problem is not merely favourable coverage. It is the abandonment of scrutiny: governments are praised, opponents vilified and inconvenient questions suppressed.

As the saying goes, “A dog with a bone in its mouth cannot bark.”

Second: Independence from corporate and commercial interests.

Concentration of media ownership, dependence on advertising and commercial pressures can determine editorial priorities. The same business interests may have stakes in media, access to public finance and influence over political decisions.

Between FY2015 and FY2024, scheduled commercial banks wrote off approximately ₹16.35 lakh crore in bad loans, of which around ₹10 lakh crore was linked to big business houses.

Yet, where is the sustained media scrutiny? Where are the investigations into the beneficiaries and the accountability of those responsible?

When the powerful can influence both the flow of public money and the flow of public information, accountability itself is compromised.

Third: Independence of Journalists from Financial Vulnerability.

Journalists must receive fair and assured remuneration and reasonable employment security. Inadequate wages and precarious employment expose them to inducements and pressures that compromise their professional independence. Fair remuneration and employment security are therefore essential safeguards of independent journalism.

Fair remuneration is not merely an employment obligation; it is an essential safeguard of independent journalism.

Fourth: Independence from ideological and religious influence.

Journalists are entitled to personal political, ideological and religious convictions. But personal beliefs must never become professional prejudices. Ideology must not determine which facts are reported, which victims deserve sympathy or which perpetrators are spared scrutiny.

A journalist who applies different standards according to political allegiance or religious identity is practising partisanship, not independent journalism.

The most dangerous form of media control is not always censorship of what is published. It is control over what is never allowed to become a subject of public scrutiny.

Press independence must therefore be both institutional and intellectual: freedom from external control and freedom from prejudices that compromise professional judgment.

4. SELECTIVE JOURNALISM

Media capture by political, corporate and ideological interests has a direct consequence: selective journalism. Some events are amplified, others buried; some victims command national outrage, while others disappear from public consciousness.
Let me cite five examples.

First: Naxalism and Maoist insurgency.

For decades, sections of the intellectual and media establishment romanticised Naxalite and Maoist insurgents as revolutionaries and champions of the oppressed.

Marginalised populations have suffered genuine injustice, exploitation and deprivation. Their grievances deserve redressal. But reporting those grievances is fundamentally different from romanticising armed groups that exploit them to advance a violent, anti-democratic ideology.

Did the media adequately expose how deprivation and alienation were exploited to recruit cadres and perpetuate violence?

When journalism romanticises violent ideologies and neglects their victims, it risks becoming a propaganda instrument and force-multiplier for the very forces it ought to expose.

Second: The genocide and religious cleansing of Kashmiri Hindus.

The genocide and religious cleansing of Kashmiri Hindus from their ancestral homeland remain one of the darkest and most shameful chapters in democratic India's history. Hindus were subjected to targeted killings, terror, threats and religious persecution. An entire Hindu community was driven out of Kashmir, and the Indian State was complicit.

And what did the Indian media do? Where was its outrage? Where were its investigations and sustained campaigns for justice and the safe return of the displaced?

The media's failure was not simply inadequate coverage. It was a complicit silence in the face of the genocide and religious cleansing of an entire community.

By its silence, the media helped erase the suffering of Kashmiri Hindus from the national conscience. That is an indictment of the media as much as it is of the State.

Third: The religious persecution of Hindus in the Northeast.

In the Christian-majority states of Mizoram and Meghalaya, Hindus have been facing severe religious persecution and discrimination. In some instances, they have been denied even the basic right to perform the last rites of their dead, to cremate their own family members in accordance with their religious traditions.

What could be more fundamental than this right? And where is the national media? Where are the headlines, investigations and expressions of outrage?

When the media turns a blind eye to the persecution of a community, it abandons the victims and shields the perpetrators from scrutiny.

Fourth: Double standards in reporting religiously sensitive crimes.

There is a glaring asymmetry in crime reporting. When the victim is Christian or Muslim, or the accused is Hindu, religious identity is often prominently highlighted. But when Hindus are victims, or the accused is Christian or Muslim, that identity disappears into generic descriptions or silence.

Why should the same journalistic standards not apply to everyone?

I demand equal seriousness of investigation, prominence of coverage and accountability, irrespective of the community involved.

The test of secular journalism is not whether it ignores religion, but whether it applies the same standards of fairness and scrutiny to everyone.

Fifth: Neutrality Must Not Become Complicity.

The media cannot be neutral between the perpetrator and the victim. Silence in the face of oppression emboldens the perpetrator and abandons the victim. Neutrality that fails to distinguish between the two is not impartiality; it is complicity.

Journalistic independence demands an unwavering commitment to truth and equal scrutiny of every government, political party, ideology and institution, irrespective of whose interests are affected.

5. FREEDOM AFTER SPEECH

A remark attributed to Idi Amin, the former President of Uganda, captures a fundamental danger: “There is freedom of speech, but I cannot guarantee freedom after speech.”

It exposes the hollowness of a freedom that exists only so long as it does not inconvenience those in power.

This brings me to an important constitutional proposition.

Article 19(1)(a), while guaranteeing freedom of speech and expression, is not adequate by itself to provide the explicit institutional recognition and safeguards that an independent Press requires. The Constitution must recognise the Free Press as an independent Fourth Estate of our democracy.

As National President of the Sarvjan Sanatan Party @sarvjansp, I affirm our commitment to pursuing a constitutional amendment to provide explicit constitutional recognition and status to the Press, so that not only freedom of speech but, importantly, freedom after speech is constitutionally guaranteed and enforced.

If the Press is indispensable to democracy, why should its institutional independence and constitutional status remain without explicit constitutional recognition?

I leave this question before this distinguished gathering.

Thank you.

🚨 DAY 3: When Congress Tried To Control The India Press!

Rahul Gandhi repeatedly alleges media bias, declining press freedom, and the media's failure to question the government, even though much of the media is openly critical of the government and continues to remain loyal to the dynasty. But what does history tell us about the state of press freedom when Congress itself was in power?

Here are THREE documented incidents worth revisiting!

🔴 1976-Four News Agencies Merged Into One!

During Emergency, four major news agencies-PTI, UNI, Hindustan Samachar and Samachar Bharati-were merged into a single entity called Samachar to ensure widespread press censorship and impose government restrictions on journalism, controlling what news reached the public.

Imagine if this happened today-Suppose the Central Government pressured independent news agencies like PTI, ANI, UNI and IANS to merge into one organisation under government influence. That is exactly what happened back then!

The merger was eventually reversed in April 1978, after the Janata Party government came to power.

🔴 1982-When Congress Tried to Jail Journalists!

31 July 1982: The Congress government in Bihar passed the Bihar Press Bill.

What did the bill propose? It sought to empower authorities to arrest journalists, editors and publishers for publishing material deemed offensive, scandalous or intended for blackmail.

What did this mean? Reports exposing corruption, misconduct or political scandals could be labelled offensive or scandalous, while investigative reports damaging politician's reputation could be portrayed as attempts to pressure or blackmail officials.

The punishment? Up to 2 years in prison for a first offence and 5 years for repeat offences, with non bailable charges!

Imagine this happening today! If government introduces a law allowing journalists to be arrested without a warrant and denied bail simply because authorities classify their reporting as offensive or scandalous. That is exactly what happened back then!

The bill sparked massive nationwide protests by journalists and opposition parties, eventually forcing Congress to withdraw it in 1983.

🔴 1988-When Rajiv Gandhi Tried to Restrict Press Freedom!

August 1988: The Congress government led by Rajiv Gandhi introduced the Defamation Bill in Parliament.

What did the bill propose? It sought to introduce new criminal offences for publishing false accusations or material considered defamatory or scandalous, with provisions to punish critical reporting, including investigations into corruption.

What could this mean? Journalists exposing corruption, misconduct or abuse of power could face criminal prosecution if politicians challenged their reports as false or defamatory. Even evidence based investigations could face legal harassment, discouraging journalists from questioning those in power.

Imagine this happening today! Suppose the Central Government introduced a similar law. Imagine the nationwide outrage, protests and accusations of dictatorship that the same Congress would unleash in the name of defending press freedom!

Nevertheless, the bill sparked nationwide protests by journalists, editors and opposition parties at the time.

Following massive opposition, the Rajiv Gandhi government announced the withdrawal of the bill in September 1988.

Three different years. Three different actions by three Congress governments. One recurring pattern: Attempts to control the press, restrict independent journalism and decide how much freedom the media should be allowed to exercise.

Rahul Gandhi's criticism of media deserves scrutiny alongside his own party's historical record.

Press freedom means defending independent journalism, not just when it suits your political interests.

History must not be forgotten simply because it is politically inconvenient! 🤡

By Skye Jacobs  Today 2:36 PM    
Your ChatGPT conversations could end up in court, and they're not protected
Chatbot conversations lack the legal privilege covering communications with lawyers, doctors, and therapists

 Add TechSpot 
   📷
Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years.  
 TechSpot means tech analysis and advice you can trust.
The takeaway: Private  conversations with AI chatbots are increasingly being used in court  cases, creating a new source of evidence for police, prosecutors, and  civil litigants. These records can expose a user's intentions, private  thoughts, and sensitive disclosures, yet they generally receive none of  the legal confidentiality protections afforded to conversations with  lawyers, doctors, or therapists.
ChatGPT and similar tools are often used for personal questions, legal worries, health concerns, and emotional support. Those conversations can feel private, but they may be accessible through a phone search, a  subpoena, discovery in a lawsuit, or a report by the AI company itself.

A review by The Washington Post found chatbot conversations cited in  12 public court cases over the past two years. The number is likely  higher because much of the evidence collected during investigations and  lawsuits never becomes public.

One case involved a teenager identified in court records as R.K.C.,  who sued Meta, Snap, TikTok, and YouTube in 2023. He alleged that their  platforms contributed to social media addiction and mental health  problems.

Defense lawyers obtained his ChatGPT history during the case. In one  October 2024 conversation, R.K.C. asked the chatbot to explain a  statement from his father about a possible settlement.

"My dad Said that I'm will get a settlement worth of  1million dollar," he wrote. "He said that If that doesn't make me happy  what does. What does he mean."

// Related Stories

 Ring rolls out new encryption system that could limit what it can hand over to police 
 AI is driving an "expertise recession" as people increasingly question professional advice 

R.K.C.'s lawyers settled with Snap, TikTok, and YouTube by late July.  They also dropped the case against Meta, saying they were concerned  about putting the teenager through a long trial. The companies denied  his claims. Mike Morgan, a partner at Morgan & Morgan, said the  ChatGPT messages did not affect the outcome of the case.
📷

Credit: The Washington Post

Morgan said young people may share more with a  chatbot than they would with family members, friends, or therapists. "A  fifteen-year-old may type things into a chatbot that he may not say to a  therapist, a parent, or a friend, and he does it without realizing that  it could end up in a defense expert's report," he said in a statement.

Chatbot records have also become part of criminal cases.

In Palm Beach County, Florida, OpenAI contacted the  FBI after a ChatGPT user repeatedly described plans to harm an  ex-girlfriend, according to a police affidavit. The FBI passed the  information to local police, who identified the woman and found that the  user, Darren Zhou, had sent her anonymous messages after their  relationship ended.

Police said the ChatGPT conversations supported the  credibility of the threats. Zhou was arrested in May and charged with  stalking and making electronic threats. He pleaded guilty this month and  was sentenced to eight years of probation.

OpenAI has said it uses software to detect  conversations that may involve dangerous behavior. Those conversations  can be reviewed by staff. If reviewers determine there is "an imminent  and credible risk of harm to others," the company may contact law  enforcement.

The company has not said how often it makes such  reports. Its transparency data, however, shows a sharp increase in  government and law-enforcement requests for user information. OpenAI  disclosed data from more than 80 accounts during the second half of  2025, more than four times the total from the same period a year  earlier.

In many cases, police do not need to obtain records from an AI company. They find the conversations on a person's phone.

Michael Price, litigation director of the Fourth  Amendment Center at the National Association of Criminal Defense  Lawyers, said people often agree to let officers search their phones. In  most situations, people have the right to refuse a search unless police  have a warrant.

"The short answer is that most people consent," Price told The Washington Post. "They shouldn't, but they do."

📷

That happened in the case of Ryan Schaefer, a  Missouri State University student accused of damaging 17 cars in a  campus parking lot. According to police records, Schaefer agreed to let  officers search his phone. They found ChatGPT messages he sent shortly  after the alleged vandalism.

"How f----d am i bro," Schaefer wrote. "What if i smahsed the s--- oitta mutlipls cars."

He later wrote: "Is there any way they could know it was me."

Schaefer later pleaded guilty to felony property damage and was sentenced in July to five years of probation.

AI chats can also be pulled into civil lawsuits  through the discovery process. In a Michigan employment case, a tire  salesman's former employer alleged that he had taken customers after  joining a rival company. The salesman had asked ChatGPT whether deleted  Yahoo emails could still be retrieved, including through a court  subpoena.

The employer argued that the messages showed he had  tried to hide evidence. A judge later ordered him to pay an undetermined  amount in attorneys' fees and allowed the lawsuit to continue.

Chatbot exchanges do not have the legal protections  that apply to conversations with lawyers, doctors, or therapists. OpenAI  CEO Sam Altman has said AI conversations should have stronger privacy  protections because people increasingly use chatbots for sensitive  matters. Courts have not recognized that type of privilege.

A federal judge in New York made that clear in a case  involving financial executive Bradley Heppner. Heppner argued that  prosecutors should not be allowed to review his conversations with  Anthropic's Claude about potential fraud defenses. The judge ruled that  the chats were not protected because Claude is not a lawyer and  Heppner's attorneys had not told him to consult the chatbot.

Heppner was convicted in May of securities fraud, wire fraud, and other charges.

The issue may grow as AI tools take on more tasks for  users and gain access to more personal data. Andrew Ferguson, a law  professor at George Washington University who studies digital  surveillance, said chatbot records may be only the beginning.

"Your entire world is going to now be available for police," Ferguson said.

"Whoever films, I'll break their mother's bones": Teen beaten by inspectors, but case closed | Documentation

A 17-year-old who boarded a bus in Jerusalem without a Rav-Kav transit card confronted four inspectors who attacked him and threatened other passengers. Although part of the incident was captured on video, the police closed the case, explaining: "The conduct of all involved parties was taken into consideration." The complainant has filed an appeal.

Gilad Cohen | Published: 11.17.26 

The police have closed an investigation file against four bus inspectors who were filmed about a year and a half ago beating a 17-year-old who confronted them on Egged bus line 39A in Jerusalem. In footage obtained by ynet, one of the inspectors is seen threatening passengers who filmed the incident: 

"Whoever films—I'll break their mother's bones. Take out your phone and delete the videos right now." The teenager filed an appeal against the decision to close the case, and police stated that the matter is under review by the State Attorney’s Appeals Department.

The incident took place on the evening of March 10, 2025. The complainant boarded an Egged bus on Herzl Boulevard in Jerusalem and stated he only realized then that he did not have his Rav-Kav card with him. A few stops later, the four inspectors boarded and began checking passengers. When they reached the teenager and he stated he had no card, a confrontation broke out during which he was struck.

In the footage, one of the inspectors can be heard shouting at him, "Sit down quietly, why did you touch me?", to which the teen replies, "I didn't touch you." At one point, the inspector yells, "I'll f*** your mother." The teen says, "I'm sorry... I'm deleting everything, don't hit me."
According to the appeal, filed via attorney Haim Bleicher from the Honenu organization, the inspectors forcibly took a camera from one of the female passengers, deleted the footage, and forced her and the other passengers off the bus while cursing at them. They instructed the driver to continue driving. 

From that moment on, it is claimed, the teenager was left alone with the inspectors, who beat him in the face and body and deleted the videos he had recorded on his mobile phone.

The teenager claims that the first part of the assault was recorded on the inspectors' body cameras, but at a certain point, they turned them off, and three of them continued to beat him for long minutes. One of them, it is claimed, tore his wallet, pulled out his identity card, and issued him a fine. According to him, they put him off at a station on Golda Meir Boulevard, which was empty at that hour. He started walking until he noticed the inspectors had returned to him, asked him for the fine form, and one of them tore off the part containing the inspector's details.

According to the appeal, at this point, they offered him a deal: "Let's make an agreement, you won't complain about us and we won't complain about you." The teen says he stayed silent out of fear. He recounts that before they boarded another bus, one of them pulled out a badge and told him he was an undercover police officer.

Only two hours later, around midnight and on the advice of his lawyer, he called the police. According to him, the dispatcher directed him to submit an online complaint, but since he could not do so, he arrived at the station the next day to file a complaint and asked for the evidence to be collected before it could be deleted. As a result of the assault, he suffered jaw pain and was sent for medical examinations and x-rays.

🚨 SERIOUS ROAD SAFETY CONCERNS INVOLVING AN UBER DRIVER IN NEW ZEALAND — AND UBER'S RESPONSE HAS BEEN EXTREMELY DISAPPOINTING.

@Uber @Uber_Support @NZPolice @NZTAMain @NZTACWC

I need some answers regarding an extremely serious road safety incident involving an Uber driver in New Zealand, and I am hoping that bringing public attention to this matter will finally result in it being properly investigated.

What happened?

During a recent Uber Pool journey, I noticed that my driver was listening to a YouTube video on his phone.

Initially, I had absolutely no issue with this. Listening to YouTube audio is no different from listening to Spotify or another music or audio service.

However, he was not simply listening to YouTube. He was actively watching the videos while driving.

I repeatedly observed him glancing at his phone screen rather than maintaining his full attention on the road.

Things became significantly more concerning when the video finished.

While the vehicle was still moving, the driver began physically scrolling through YouTube, browsing videos and selecting something else to watch or listen to.

He was doing this while transporting me as a paying passenger.

As if that wasn't concerning enough, there was another extremely serious problem.

HIS PHONE WAS MOUNTED DIRECTLY OVER HIS INTERIOR REAR-VIEW MIRROR, COMPLETELY BLOCKING IT AND RENDERING IT UNUSABLE.

This was not simply somebody briefly holding their phone in front of a mirror.

He had a phone holder installed in a position that obstructed his rear-view mirror.

Think about that for a moment.

This wasn't a temporary obstruction caused by somebody accidentally moving something into the wrong position.

The equipment had been deliberately installed in that location.

Someone had to position the holder, secure it and place the phone into it.

That requires preparation. The resulting obstruction wasn't simply a momentary lapse in judgement.

This raises serious concerns about whether the vehicle was being operated in compliance with New Zealand road safety requirements.

Combined with watching YouTube and actively scrolling through his phone while driving, I believe this behaviour created an unacceptable risk to passengers and other road users.

He could have caused a serious collision, potentially injuring or killing somebody.

What evidence do I have?

I took photographs and recorded video evidence of the incident.

The photograph attached to this post shows the driver's phone mounted at the rear-view mirror, with YouTube displayed on the screen and his hand physically interacting with it.

Obviously, a still photograph cannot demonstrate that a vehicle was moving.

However, I also have the original video recording, which shows the incident occurring while the vehicle was in motion.

I am deliberately NOT publishing that video publicly at this stage.

Why?

Because the footage contains potentially identifying information, including the driver's appearance, and I do not want to expose his identity to the public unnecessarily.

I also want to protect my own privacy.

This is about road safety and accountability, not encouraging people to identify, harass or dox somebody.

The full, original footage is available to the appropriate authorities, and I am more than willing to cooperate with any formal investigation.

What did Uber do?

I reported the incident to Uber through its safety reporting system, explaining exactly what I witnessed and providing access to the video evidence.

Uber initially informed me that it would review the driver's account and ensure I would not be matched with him again.

That's wonderful. I certainly don't want to travel with him again.

BUT WHAT ABOUT EVERYONE ELSE?

What about the next paying passenger?

What about other motorists?

What about cyclists and pedestrians?

Preventing me from being matched with this driver again does absolutely nothing to address the wider safety concerns.

text:
Delhi Police asks X to take down IFF's account and posts. IFF will challenge the notices in court unless they are withdrawn.

The Delhi Police has asked X to remove the Internet Freedom Foundation's account, six of its posts, the accounts of SFLC and @geoblockedindia, and posts by 16 other users, on the ground that they defame the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. The posts document and comment on a legal notice sent in the RSS's name to IFF, SFLC and @geoblockedindia, which demanded that the three stop criticising and documenting government blocking orders. IFF received copies of the two police notices from X on the morning of 3 November 2026.
IFF calls on the Delhi Police to withdraw both notices. If they are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court.

What has happened

On 29 October 2026 at 9:54 PM, IFF, SFLC and the operator of @geoblockedindia received a two-page "legal notice" said to be issued on behalf of the RSS. It asked the three to stop opposing the government's blocking directions, stop documenting restricted content, stop posting details of geo-blocked posts, and confirm in writing within seven days that they would comply. It was signed by an unnamed "Authorised Signatory". Several RSS office-bearers have since said on X that the notice is not authentic. IFF replied to the notice, wrote to the RSS at its official address asking whether it had authorised it, and published both the notice and its reply on 30 October.

On 31 October 2026 at 8:06 PM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police, filed an "Illegal Content Report" with X (reference LD-321926). It listed two posts: IFF's post of 30 October on the notice, and SFLC post of the same day. The stated reason was that the posts are "defamatory towards the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023". The boxes for "safety/security", "defamation" and "other" were ticked. The fields for the nature of the court order and court order details were left empty. The desired action was "Remove/withhold content".

On 1 November 2026, a second notice arrived in the RSS's name. It said the matter had been handed to the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, that complaints had been filed in several states, and that requests had been made to block IFF's X account and suspend the organisations. The Delhi Police had made its first request to X the previous evening. IFF did not know this until X told it on 3 November.

On 2 November 2026 at 8:51 AM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) filed a second notice with X (reference LD-322956). It lists 40 URLs. Thirty-seven are posts. Three are the entire accounts of @internetfreedom, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. This time the boxes for "Hate speech", "defamation", "safety/security", "enforcement of court order" and "other" were all ticked. The court order fields were again left empty. The stated reason reads: "The posts constitute defamation and illegal content under Section 356 BNS. Under Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, read with Section 79(3)(b) IT Act, lawful notices require action within 3 hours."

The 16 other users are @ProdctiveUseful, @PanjwaniManoj, @jidge_, @RatanSharda55, @baxiabhishek, @SchrdingersDbag, @ashleshbiradar, @seemay, @NasirHussainINC, @Being_creat_ive, @AjoyDharmavaram, @othlaw, @_ananyaaa, @AimPoojaind, @incorigibleBhai and @rraoind. Their posts, as far as IFF can tell, comment on the notice or on the notice about it.

X forwarded both notice to IFF on 3 November 2026, at 8:47 AM and 10:03 AM, saying it was doing so "in the interest of transparency" and that IFF may wish to seek legal counsel and challenge the request in court. X's emails do not say that it has acted on the requests. The Delhi Police has not written to IFF, and no court has been approached, as far as the reports disclose. SFLC and @geoblockedindia have separately reported notifications from X about requests from the Uttar Pradesh Police, the Telangana Police and the Delhi Police's Cyber Crime unit, one of them against the whole of the @geoblockedindia account.

IFF's position

IFF condemns this legal action. A police force has made itself the enforcement arm of a private legal notice whose authenticity the organisation it names has not confirmed, and whose demand was that three organisations stop documenting censorship. The notices would deliver exactly what the notice asked for as they would also remove the accounts of the three groups in India that keep public records of what is blocked, and of who ordered it.

The posts in question are about a legal notice sent to us. They quote it, criticise how it was drafted, and say that we will carry on with our work. A person who receives a threat is entitled to publish it and answer it and that is not defamation of the sender. 

In the three weeks before the first notice, IFF assisted 86 people whose accounts were suspended or whose posts were withheld in India. SFLC's Free Speech Tracker recorded about 268 content restrictions and 83 account restrictions in the first 29 days of October. @geoblockedindia publishes the orders behind such blocks when platforms disclose them. None of this is unlawful. Documenting censorship and challenging it in court is what the Constitution expects of citizens.
IFF will not delete the posts. If the Delhi Police does not withdraw the notices, we will challenge them in court.

Why the reports are unlawful

Defamation is not a police matter. Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is a non-cognizable and bailable offence. Under Section 222 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, no court can take cognizance of it except on a complaint by the person aggrieved. 

Under Section 174 of the BNSS, the police cannot investigate a non-cognizable offence without an order of a Magistrate. The Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) is not the person aggrieved. The notices disclose no complaint by the RSS and no order of any Magistrate. Whether a statement is defamatory is for a court to decide after hearing its author, with the defences of truth, fair comment and good faith available to that author. 

In Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India, (2016) 7 SCC 221, the Supreme Court upheld criminal defamation on the strength of these safeguards. A police officer who asks a platform to remove speech as defamatory has decided the question himself, without a complainant, a court or a hearing.

The posts are protected comment. Exceptions 1 to 3 to Section 356(1) protect the truth published for the public good, opinion on the public conduct of public servants, and opinion on the conduct of any person touching a public question. The posts publish a notice that was sent to us and give our opinion of it. The RSS, if it sent the notice, chose to enter a public question. If it did not, the posts defame no one.

Further, Section 79(3)(b) and Rule 3(1)(d) do not permit this. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down Section 79(3)(b) so that an intermediary acquires "actual knowledge" only through a court order, or a notification from the appropriate government or its agency that unlawful acts relatable to Article 19(2) are being committed. The court said that it would be difficult for intermediaries to judge the legitimacy of the millions of requests they receive, and that the burden must not be placed on them. Rule 3(1)(d), as amended in November 2025 and February 2026, now requires the intimation to come from an officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary or Deputy Inspector General, to be reasoned, and to specify the legal basis and the nature of the unlawful act, subject to a monthly review by a Secretary-level officer. The three-hour window the notice invokes applies to a lawful order that meets these conditions. A web form that ticks "hate speech" and "enforcement of court order" while leaving the court order fields blank, and that gives one sentence of reasons for 40 URLs, is not such an order.

The notices by the Delhi Police are disproportionate. They seek to remove three accounts in their entirety, with years of posts, over six, four and eleven posts respectively. They sweep in 16 third parties whose only connection is that they commented on a public controversy. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that any restriction on speech must be necessary, proportionate and the least restrictive measure available, and that orders restricting speech must be published and reasoned. Removing an organisation's entire account for criticising a legal notice fails each of these tests.

The effect is to silence documentation of censorship and providing legal aid to Indian internet users. The accounts named are those that record blocking orders in India. The notice asked them to stop. A takedown request that accomplishes the demand of an anonymous private notice is not law enforcement. It is the use of state power for a private end, which Article 14 forbids.

Our demands

1. To the Delhi Police: Withdraw reports LD-321926 and LD-322956 and confirm the withdrawal in writing to X and to IFF. 

2. To the Delhi Police: Disclose the complaint on which the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) acted, the authority under which the reports were filed, and whether any order of a Magistrate under Section 174 BNSS exists. Disclose every request made to any platform in this matter, including those made by the Cyber Crime unit against @geoblockedindia.

3. To X: Do not act on the reports. If any content is withheld in India, tell the affected user before acting, give them the full request, and name the legal basis. Publish both reports to the Lumen database, as the reporting form itself contemplates.

4. To the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and the Ministry of Home Affairs: Have the Secretary-level review required by Rule 3(1)(d) examine these intimations, and tell police forces that Rule 3(1)(d) is not a remedy for defamation, which the law reserves to the person aggrieved and to the courts.

5. To the RSS: State publicly whether it authorised either notice or any complaint to the police. If it did not, say so to the Delhi Police.

If the notices are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court. We will continue to document blocking orders, to publish them, and to provide legal assistance to anyone whose account or post is withheld in India. Nothing in these notices changes that.

text:
Can your wife get your foreign visa cancelled by complaining to an embassy about a matrimonial dispute in India?

In my experience, most such complaints do not result in any action by the embassy. The complainant may simply be advised to pursue remedies through the Indian police and judicial system.

However, I have encountered exceptions.

In one case, my client's US visa was cancelled after his wife complained to the American Embassy about alleged dowry harassment in India, even though he was visiting the United States at the time.

Another client received a show-cause notice from a foreign embassy following a complaint.

These situations are uncommon in my experience, but they demonstrate that complaints arising from matrimonial disputes can sometimes have immigration consequences.

Ultimately, visa decisions are governed by the laws and immigration authorities of the country concerned. No Indian lawyer can guarantee how a foreign embassy will respond to such allegations.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

text:
Last night IFF, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia received a legal notice said to be issued purportedly on behalf of the RSS. It’s hard to believe this comes from an organisation that has had a century to practise its paperwork and hence this may even be a weird prank! This notice asks us to stop criticising the Government’s blocking orders and stop documenting them. It also wants us to confirm in writing within seven days (seriously).

We can tell it’s an excellent teaching aid and here are seven lessons from it.

1) Say who you are: The notice names no advocate and gives no enrollment number. It is signed by an “Authorised Signatory” with no name. Replies go to a free Proton Mail ID, and the “office” is a residential flat in outer Delhi. A notice that can’t tell you who sent it is less a legal document than a weather event.

2) Have a grievance of your own: It never says how its client is harmed when we criticise a MeitY advisory. It complains on behalf of the Government’s blocking orders. The Union has no shortage of lawyers, and it hasn’t asked for volunteers.

3) Name the law: It threatens “appropriate legal action” under “the applicable provisions of law” and doesn’t cite a single section of any statute. A threat with no law, is literally an empty threat.

4) Don’t ask people to give up a fundamental right within seven days: The first demand is that we stop “publicly opposing” government directions. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court held that discussion and advocacy of a cause, however unpopular, sit at the heart of Article 19(1)(a). Opposing an order is how its legality gets tested. That is the Constitution working as intended.

5) Check whether the courts asked for the thing you want stopped” In Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Supreme Court held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be made available so people can challenge them. The Reddit order is on the public Lumen Database because Reddit put it there. Reading a public database and saying what’s in it has a name. It’s called research.

6) Show us the spark and the powder keg: The notice says our work weakens national security measures, but it gives no instance, date or harm. In S. Rangarajan (1989), the Supreme Court held that the danger feared from speech can’t be remote, conjectural or far-fetched. It has to be like a spark in a powder keg. A post about a Lumen filing is not a spark.

7) Read it once more before you press send: The paragraphs run 1, then an empty 2 and 3, then 4. A PIN code wanders into the facts. The account it targets is on “Twitter”. 

Our reply is short. The notice is legally deficient because it makes no material allegation and cites no illegality. We will respectfully continue to advance constitutional rights, as we have done before. Notices like this rarely expect to win in court. They expect the recipient to get tired. We often are tired, but it has never changed what we do. Solidarity with @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. 

If your post or account has been blocked in India, write to legal@internetfreedom.in.

PUBLIC STATEMENT BY PARANJOY GUHA THAKURTA
On the arbitrary takedown of https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe by Hostinger following legal notices from Indiabulls founder Sameer Gehlaut
October 31, 2026
On the morning of October 28, 2026, my website https://t.co/OeAAoTPXCy and all its associated subdomains, including https://t.co/I8kylhDXVk and https://t.co/D8b6LtNzWD, were abruptly taken offline by our web hosting provider, Hostinger (HOSTINGER operations, UAB). The website, registered twelve years ago, serves as an online archive of my work over several decades as a journalist, author, publisher, and maker of documentary films and music videos
Hostinger gave no prior intimation, warning, or opportunity to respond before suspending the entire hosting account. When my colleague contacted Hostinger “Support” at 6:48 AM on October 28, a hosting “specialist” stated that the suspension was triggered by an abuse report for "Fraud/Scam" and declared that "unsuspension is not negotiable in this case."
This sudden shutdown of an entire repository under the label "Fraud/Scam" happened just days after Sameer Gehlaut, founder of the Indiabulls group, served me with an ex parte court order demanding the removal of a single article published more than seven years on https://t.co/25noyNupwJ.
For over six years, Indiabulls and Shri Gehlaut have pursued legal action over this report and I have consistently defended our journalistic report in court. Here is the timeline:
·  March 11, 2020: Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited filed a criminal defamation complaint (CC No. 1765/2020) before the Patiala House Courts, New Delhi, against NewsClick, its Reader's Editor Urmilesh, co-author of the article Sourodipto Sanyal, NewsClick editor Prabir Purkayastha, and me over an article published on the website on September 30, 2019.
·  June 6, 2025 and July 9, 2025: More than five years after the complaint was filed, a Judicial Magistrate at Patiala House Courts passed an order on June 6, 2025, dropping proceedings against Shri Purkayastha while issuing summons to the remaining four accused, including me, under Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code. A formal summons was issued on July 9, 2025, for appearance on July 30, 2025.
·  August 27, 2026: Counsel for Shri Gehlaut, sent me a legal notice demanding the takedown of the article within 24 to 48 hours, claiming that a status report by the Economic Offences Wing (EOW) of the Delhi Police had altered the factual position.
·  September 2, 2026: My counsel sent a reply pointing out concerns with the legal notice
·  October 24, 2026: Indiabulls Nests Limited (Plaintiff No. 1) and Sameer Gehlaut (Plaintiff No. 2) obtained an ex parte ad interim injunction from the Court of one of the District and Sessions Judges, Patiala House Courts, New Delhi, in Civil Suit No. 529/2026 (Indiabulls Nests Ltd. & Anr. v. Ashok Kumar/John Doe & Ors.), in which I am arrayed as Defendant No. 19. The order directed the removal and de-indexing of the article on https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe (listed as Item A-33 in Schedule A).
·  October 25, 2026 (10:13 AM IST): Advocates representing Indiabulls Nests Limited and Sameer Gehlaut, emailed me the October 24 court order and suit documents, demanding immediate deletion and written confirmation of compliance.
·  October 26, 2026 (11:33 PM IST): Sameer Gehlaut personally sent an email from his official address (sameer@indiabulls.com) demanding the immediate deletion of the URL from https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe and threatening to move the court under Order XXXIX Rule 2A of the Code of Civil Procedure if I did not comply, noting that the matter is next listed on December 18, 2026. While I was in the process of challenging the order dated 24.10.2026 before higher forums, on the same day, advocates representing Shri Gehlaut submitted a court order takedown complaint to Google LLC.

·  October 28, 2026 (3:16 PM IST): Google Search Console sent an automated notice ([WNC-598900]) informing me that Google was blocking the specific URL https://t.co/SsSVUVLKGX  from appearing in search results on https://t.co/2IOZ4I1WqC.

The Lumen Database record of this complaint (Notice ID: 101001876) reveals the scale of the takedown request. The complaint targeted 52 URLs on websites across major national and international news organisations, including The Economic Times, Business Standard, The Caravan, The Daily Pioneer, Business Today, Deccan Herald, ET Now, Financial Express, Livemint, Moneycontrol, Moneylife, NDTV Profit, The New Indian Express, Outlook Business, The Quint, Quartz, and NewsClick, along with posts on X (formerly Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and Scribd.

Most of these reports on major corporate news websites remain accessible online. In fact, Item 39 on the Lumen takedown list is the original September 30, 2019 article published on https://t.co/qQP2N2fxA2: https://t.co/hgneAPvDuF, which remains live and accessible  as of now.

Yet, in the case of https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe, the entire domain and every website hosted on my account were wiped off the internet.

Hostinger's Baseless "Fraud/Scam" Claim and Demand for Accountability

Hostinger did not cite the Patiala House Courts order when it suspended my account on October 28, 2026. Instead, its representative claimed that the hosting account was permanently suspended due to an abuse report for "Fraud/Scam".

This allegation is demonstrably false:

1. VirusTotal Security Analysis: Independent domain checks conducted on October 28, 2026, at 7:48 AM and 7:54 AM on VirusTotal confirm that 0 out of 92 security vendors flagged https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe or https://t.co/I8kylhDXVk as malicious, phishing, or fraudulent. VirusTotal explicitly categorises https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe under "news and media".

2. Google Safe Browsing Status: Checks on the Google Safe Browsing diagnostic tool at 7:55 AM and 7:56 AM on October 28, 2026, for both https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe and https://t.co/D8b6LtNzWD returned the status: "No unsafe content found".
My website https://t.co/OeAAoTPXCy does not sell financial products, solicit funds for commercial schemes, or engage in any activity that could remotely be classified as a scam. It is a repository of public-interest journalism, books, documentary films, and investigative reports built over a lifetime of work. By acting on a fabricated "Fraud/Scam" abuse report without a single verification check or prior notice to the domain owner, Hostinger has allowed its abuse-reporting mechanism to be weaponised to censor an independent journalist.
Even where a court order directs the removal or de-indexing of a specific URL, a web hosting provider has no legal or ethical justification to pull down an entire domain and hundreds of unrelated articles, archives, and subdomains without notice.
I demand immediate answers and accountability from Hostinger:
1. Who submitted the false "Fraud/Scam" abuse report against https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe, and on what exact date and time was it received?
2. What internal verification did Hostinger's abuse team conduct before classifying a 12-year-old journalism portal as a "Fraud/Scam" site, especially when 92 security vendors on VirusTotal and Google Safe Browsing show zero malicious or unsafe content?
3. Why was no prior notice, warning, or copy of the complaint sent to me before suspending the entire hosting account?
4. On what basis did Hostinger's specialist declare that the suspension of an entire archive of journalistic work is "not negotiable"?
While my legal advisers are in the process of taking appropriate steps in court regarding the ex parte order dated October 24, 2026, and the wholesale suspension of my website, this backdoor censorship through web hosting providers sets a dangerous precedent for the independence of the media and freedom of expression as enshrined in Article (19)(1)(a) of the Constitution of India as a fundamental right of every citizen of India.
Yours sincerely

Paranjoy Guha Thakurta
Independent Journalist, Author, Publisher and Maker of Documentary Films and Music Videos

text:
From journalist - Ambuj Kumar

His statement, first in Hindi and then in English

पहले कमाई बंद, अब भारत में पहुंच पर रोक। एक पत्रकार को बार-बार अपनी बात रखने के लिए संघर्ष क्यों करना पड़ रहा है?

कुछ दिन पहले ही Facebook ने मेरे “Ambuj Kumar – Lokhit India” पेज को डीमोनेटाइज कर दिया था। शिकायत करने और सवाल उठाने के बाद मोनेटाइजेशन बहाल हुआ। अब आज, 9 नवंबर 2026 को, इसी नाम वाले अकाउंट पर भारत में 7 दिन की रोक की सूचना मिली है। पेज, वीडियो और फोटो तक पहुंच प्रतिबंधित करने के अलग संदेश भी आए हैं।

Facebook इन कार्रवाइयों के लिए “भारत सरकार/कानून लागू करने वाली एजेंसी” के नोटिस और स्थानीय कानूनों का हवाला दे रहा है। संदेशों में IT Act की धारा 79(3)(b) और IT Rules, 2021 के Rule 4(4) का उल्लेख है।

लेकिन मुझे मूल सरकारी नोटिस या शिकायत की प्रति नहीं दी गई। किस एजेंसी ने कार्रवाई माँगी? किस पोस्ट के किस हिस्से पर आपत्ति है? ठोस कानूनी आधार क्या है? इसकी जानकारी नहीं दी गई। केवल कानून का नाम लिख देना जवाबदेही नहीं है।

प्रभावित सामग्री में 26 सितंबर का समाचार वीडियो और 16 जून की मेरे चैनल की पहचान वाली फोटो भी शामिल है। उस फोटो पर रोक क्यों?

मेरे सीधे सवाल हैं:

1. नोटिस जारी करने वाली एजेंसी का नाम, नोटिस की तारीख, संदर्भ संख्या और उसकी प्रति कहाँ है?
2. किस सामग्री का कौन-सा कथन किस कानून का उल्लंघन करता है?
3. Facebook पहले चेतावनी देने का दावा करता है। वे चेतावनियाँ कब और कहाँ भेजी गईं? उनका रिकॉर्ड दीजिए।
4. कुछ पोस्ट पर आपत्ति के आधार पर पूरे अकाउंट/पेज की पहुंच रोकने का औचित्य क्या है?
5. क्या सामग्री और उसके पत्रकारिता संबंधी संदर्भ की मानव समीक्षा हुई?
6. पहले डीमोनेटाइजेशन, शिकायत के बाद बहाली और अब यह रोक—क्या इन अलग-अलग कार्रवाइयों की पारदर्शी समीक्षा होगी?
7. सात दिन बाद वास्तव में क्या बहाल होगा? प्रभावी अपील का रास्ता क्या है?

मैं दोनों कार्रवाइयों के बीच किसी साझा कारण का दावा नहीं कर रहा। लेकिन बार-बार होने वाली ऐसी कार्रवाइयों का मेरी पत्रकारिता, आजीविका और दर्शकों तक पहुंच पर सीधा असर पड़ता है।

स्वतंत्र पत्रकारिता को अस्पष्ट संदेशों और अपारदर्शी फैसलों के भरोसे नहीं छोड़ा जा सकता। मैं मूल नोटिस और स्पष्ट कारण उपलब्ध कराने, तत्काल मानव समीक्षा तथा अकाउंट/पेज की पहुंच बहाल करने की माँग करता हूँ।

मेरा पेज: https://t.co/MCdTKuJloF

First, my earnings were cut off; now, access to my content from within India has been blocked. Why must a journalist constantly struggle just to make their voice heard?

Just a few days ago, Facebook demonetized my page, “Ambuj Kumar – Lokhit India.” After I filed a complaint and raised questions, monetization was restored. Now, today—November 9, 2026—I have been notified that access to this same account from within India has been restricted for seven days. I have also received separate notifications stating that access to the page, as well as to specific videos and photos, has been blocked.

Facebook justifies these actions by citing notices from the “Government of India/law enforcement agencies” and local laws. The notifications reference Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 4(4) of the IT Rules, 2021.

However, I have not been provided with a copy of the original government notice or the complaint. Which agency requested this action? Which specific part of which post is being objected to? What is the concrete legal basis for this? None of this information has been shared. Simply citing a law does not constitute accountability.

The affected content includes a news video from September 26 and a photo identifying my channel, dated June 16. Why is that photo being blocked?

I have a few direct questions:

1. What is the name of the agency that issued the notice? What is the date of the notice, the reference number, and where is the copy of it?
2. Which specific statement within the content violates which law?
3. Facebook claims to provide prior warnings. When and where were these warnings sent? Please provide a record of them.
4. What is the justification for blocking access to the entire account/page based on objections to only a few posts?
5. Was there a human review of the content, taking into account its journalistic context?
6. Given the sequence of events—initial demonetization, restoration following a complaint, and now this block—will there be a transparent review of these separate actions?
7. What, exactly, will be restored after seven days? What is the path to an effective appeal?

I am not claiming that there is a common reason linking these two actions. However, such recurring actions have a direct impact on my journalism, my livelihood, and my reach to my audience.

Independent journalism cannot be left at the mercy of vague messages and opaque decisions. I demand that the original notices and clear reasons be provided, that an immediate human review be conducted, and that access to my account/page be restored.

My page: https://t.co/MCdTKuJloF

text:
**YOUR PHONE IS YOUR PRIVATE LIFE. WHO GAVE THE STATE A BLANK CHEQUE TO ACCESS IT?**

An Internet Freedom Foundation investigation has exposed a deeply troubling expansion of India's digital forensic surveillance capabilities.

The Home Ministry approved exemptions covering 422 foreign forensic items. Procurement specifications reveal technologies capable of extracting data from seized devices and using stored login tokens to access more than 100 online platforms, including WhatsApp, Instagram, Tinder and cloud services.

This is not merely a question of technology. It is a question of constitutional liberty.

A citizen's private conversations, photographs, location history, relationships and professional communications cannot become unrestricted investigative resources simply because a device has been seized.

The Supreme Court recognised privacy as a fundamental right in the Puttaswamy judgment. Yet comprehensive safeguards governing forensic extraction, data retention, access and independent oversight remain inadequate.

And accountability cannot be selective: procurement activity has also been documented in opposition-governed states. No government should enjoy unchecked surveillance powers.

National security cannot become a universal excuse for invading personal privacy. Criminal investigation requires lawful authority, necessity, proportionality and judicial safeguards.

**A democracy must protect citizens from crime without turning every citizen into a potential subject of surveillance.**

Privacy is not a privilege. It is a constitutional right. Transparency is not optional. Accountability is non-negotiable.

#DimaagiNaxal #Resistance #UnitedResistance

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

 In March 2026, ahead of the Kerala Assembly elections (polling on 9 April 2026), a 2019 Election Commission of India (ECI) letter redistributed by the Kerala Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) office was found to carry the seal of the BJP’s Kerala unit. This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. They alleged compromised institutional neutrality, claiming seals were being “casually swapped” and questioning whether the ECI and BJP shared the same “power centre.” Some BJP responses labelled the circulation of the old document as misinformation or a political plot.thewire.inDeletion of posts controversyActing on an ECI directive (under the Model Code of Conduct), the Kerala Police cyber cell issued notices to X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and numerous individual accounts. My analysis of how Indian LE traced through an unlabeled service and wrongly froze @xxxkeym's Gate account:

The case stems from a pig butchering victim who allegedly lost $1.7M of BTC, USDT, DOGE & SOL in May 2025.

Andhra Pradesh CID registered it as Cr. No. 10/2025 and filed a charge sheet in March 2026.

In July 2025, xxxkeym had Gate deposit address 17mpajZ6Nq3dG3T6wUhaXxYF4Qy9HJnYx5 frozen after depositing 15 BTC from 3NcBhqK in the following transaction:
885f3afab562251b222363cf12095e864ddb94636674b01f0cdb05997e5a54a0

This is one transaction Indian LE cites in its notice. 3NcBhqK was funded by xxxkeym's own OKX & Binance withdrawals in Jan 2023 and the coins sat dormant for years until the Gate deposit. 

Indian LE never froze his OKX or Binance accounts, the actual source of the 15 BTC, which tells you how flawed their justification is.

Gate froze his entire account, which held roughly $3M at the time and about $1.5M today.

The Indian court order hands all of it to the complainant.

Gate deposit address 17mpajZ also received two deposits for 15 BTC total in 2025 from bc1pkkwqyxn3rm608ryuqg9hyqna0syq4jx5pxkr7pzg8n3usx6tyqfst5u966, which is also controlled by xxxkeym.

bc1quzw & bc1qtu66z were reported as alibarbit[.]bit, the same scam named in Indian LE's press release. 

That was a mistake. Both belong to the Merlin Chain bridge, which is unlabeled in most compliance tools. 

xxxkeym is simply a normal Merlin user trading tokens on the L2. This wrong label is the only place the scam touches his transaction history.

xxxkeym bridged 50 BTC into Merlin on March 28, 2024, over a year before the alleged May 2025 theft.

Separately on July 15, 2025 xxxkeym had a 7 BTC private key compromise theft which was reported to local police and also SlowMist was engaged. His stolen funds flowed to Wasabi. 

This is embarrassing incompetence by Indian LE, who seem incapable of reviewing basic blockchain data.

Indian LE, the prosecutor and the judge all signed off on this, Gate froze the account, and LE did a full press release about it recently, while the real victim here (the Gate user) hasn't had access to his funds for nearly 16 months.

My hot take is VASPs need to challenge weak jurisdictions like India, Canada, etc due to repeated negligence in criminal cases.

The Kerala Government has revealed that it ordered the takedown of 15,627 posts, news cards, photographs and video links from social media platforms in the six months since it assumed office in May 2026. The figures were shared by Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala in a written reply to a question raised by Xavier Chittilappilly, MLA, in the Kerala Legislative Assembly.

The disclosure comes amid controversy over the government's role in restricting online content. In August 2026, several media organisations reported instances of their content being taken down. At the time, Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan stated at a press conference that his government had not issued any instructions to Meta to block content. Subsequent media reports suggested that some of these restrictions were caused by technical glitches.

However, the government's involvement in issuing blocking orders came to light during cases filed before the Kerala High Court by NOCAP, an independent digital media organisation, and the Kerala Independent Farmers Association (KIFA), after their Facebook pages were blocked. In both cases, the High Court ordered the restoration of the pages, observing that objections to specific posts or comments did not justify blocking an entire social media account.

These cases sparked a political controversy, with the Opposition accusing the Congress-led government of using police and administrative authorities to restrict online criticism. Questions were subsequently raised in the Legislative Assembly, leading to the disclosure of the number of takedown directions issued by the government.

Can a software-based video compression method be patented in India?

We look at Huawei’s Patent No. 558691 and assess it in light of India’s Computer Related Inventions (CRI) Guidelines.

What Do the 2025 CRI Guidelines Say?

The 2025 CRI Guidelines place greater emphasis on an invention's technical effect. This means software-based methods may be assessed based on the technical results they produce. This technical-effect test aligns with European standards, which the Parliament explicitly rejected in 2004 to prevent a “monopoly of multinationals”.

Does producing a technical result change the nature of the underlying invention? No, it does not.

Huawei’s patent still claims a way of processing information through software, via an algorithm, not a new hardware component. This raises concerns about whether the 2025 Guidelines weaken the legislative intent behind Section 3(k) of the Patents Act, 1970.

Transparency Matters

When a patent is granted, the reasoning behind the decision matters. In this case, the patent was granted without a hearing, and the Patent Controller’s detailed reasoning is not available on the Indian Patent Office website.

Without this reasoning, it is difficult to understand how the Section 3(k) objection was addressed or why the patent was considered eligible for grant.

“Say No to Software Patents” has long been https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s position. Through our Patent Watch series, we examine software patents in India and their implications for software freedom.

Read more at our blog: https://t.co/2tfgWWTvbH

The Three-Part Test Under the 2016 CRI Guidelines

The 2016 Computer Related Inventions (CRI) Guidelines set out a three-part test to assess whether a computer-related invention is patentable. These tests help limit the grant to patents that are very evidently software, as seen in our 2023 study ‘Software Patents in India: Law and Practice’

1. Examine the invention in substance, not individual claims
The patent’s core contribution is an algorithm for processing information through a neural network.

2. Check if the contribution goes beyond software or an algorithm
Although applied to video compression, the method centres on how software processes information via this neural network-based algorithm, and does not go beyond it.

3. Check if the software uses novel hardware
The patent relies on conventional processing circuitry and does not claim any new or specialised hardware.

Why Is This an Egregious Software Patent?

The patent does not claim any new or specialised hardware. Its central contribution is a software-based method of processing and combining information within a neural network.

Under the 2016 CRI Guidelines, this would not have qualified for a patent because the contribution lies in a computer programme implemented on conventional hardware. Such a rejection would also be in line with Section 3(k) of the Patents Act, 1970, which prohibits patents that are computer programmes “per se” to prevent a “monopoly of multinationals”, but the patent in question was granted under the 2025 CRI Guidelines.

The Delhi High Court has issued notice on a constitutional challenge to the automated filter which Meta operates on Instagram and Facebook in India, and to Rule 4(4) of the IT Rules, 2021. On 19 November 2026, the Court issued notice to the Union of India and to Meta on a writ petition filed by Live Law Media Private Limited and its Director, Sindhu T.P. IFF is supporting LiveLaw in this challenge. (1/10)
Read More: https://t.co/s5ichxKjPu

The petition contends that Rule 4(4) exceeds the powers conferred by the IT Act, creates a blocking regime outside Section 69A, and operates as a prior restraint on the press. A publisher whose report is suppressed by automated tools receives no notice, no reasons and no hearing. The grievance route offers little, since 54,918 appeals were pending before the Grievance Appellate Committee on 2 November 2026. (9/10)

The Court has granted the respondents four weeks to file their counter-affidavits and has listed the matter on 18 January 2027. LiveLaw seeks the striking down of Rule 4(4) to this extent, the quashing of the advisories, production of the “legal requests” and restoration of its reels. If your content has been restricted “under Rule 4(4)” or on an undisclosed “legal request”, write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We will continue to support this challenge. (10/10)
